common_name: Aromatic Snakeroot (Lesser Snakeroot, Fragrant-Leaf Woodland Ageratina)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Aromatic Snakeroot is a compact eastern US relative of white snakeroot with fragrant foliage, blooming in fall as a valuable late-season nectar source.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; more compact and better behaved in a garden setting than its larger relative white snakeroot. Aromatic Snakeroot bears small, fuzzy, white flower clusters in fall atop a tidy, well-branched clump of aromatic foliage that releases a pleasant fragrance when brushed or crushed, providing a valuable late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies at a time when few other woodland-edge natives are still blooming. Its smaller stature compared to other Eupatorium and Ageratina relatives makes it a good fit for a mixed native border rather than only a naturalized woodland setting. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Roundleaf Thoroughwort (Stalkless Gray-Green Native Pollinator Perennial)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Roundleaf Thoroughwort bears distinctive stalkless, round, gray-green paired leaves and white late-summer flowerheads that draw large numbers of native bees and butterflies.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, in a wet-to-dry woodland edge, pine savanna, or meadow setting. Roundleaf Thoroughwort is easily distinguished from other native thoroughworts by its distinctive stalkless, rounded, gray-green leaves that clasp directly against the stem in opposite pairs, topped by flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late summer that draw an unusually large and diverse crowd of native bees, wasps, and butterflies. It tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than many wetland-associated Eupatorium relatives, adapting to both damp low spots and drier woodland-edge sites. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Upland Boneset is a shade-tolerant woodland species with sessile, non-clasping leaves, distinct from wetland-loving common boneset.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, in dry to average woodland conditions rather than the consistently wet soil that common boneset prefers. Upland Boneset is a genuinely dry-adapted, shade-tolerant thoroughwort of upland woods and woodland edges, distinguished from wetland-associated Eupatorium relatives by its narrow, tapering, sessile leaves that do not clasp or fuse around the stem, topped by flat clusters of white flowers in late summer to early fall that provide valuable nectar for bees and butterflies as many other blooms fade. Its tolerance for drier, shadier conditions makes it a useful native option for a dry woodland garden where the classic wetland boneset would struggle. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Carolina Wild Indigo (Grayhairy Wild Indigo, Coastal Plain Baptisia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot; Carolina Wild Indigo is a narrow Coastal Plain and Sandhills endemic (Virginia to Georgia) with gray-hairy foliage and cream to pale yellow flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean to average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Carolina Wild Indigo is a regional Coastal Plain and Sandhills endemic, native from Virginia to Georgia, distinguished from the more widely grown Baptisia species by its distinctly gray-hairy, silvery-toned foliage and its cream to pale yellow spring flowers held on a shorter, more compact plant than white or blue wild indigo. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species while its flowers draw bumblebees, among the few pollinators strong enough to trip the flower's mechanism. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Mohr's Rosinweed is a narrow Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia endemic with shaggy-hairy foliage, a valuable late-summer nectar and pollen source for specialist bees.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; established plants tolerate drought well thanks to a deep taproot typical of the genus. Mohr's Rosinweed is a regional endemic found only in a narrow range across Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia, distinguished by its distinctly shaggy, hairy foliage and stems, bearing large, bright yellow, sunflower-like composite blooms in mid-to-late summer on tall, sturdy stalks. Like other Silphium species, its flowers are a magnet for specialist long-tongued bees and other pollinators during a period when many spring bloomers have finished, and the seed heads that follow provide food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. It is exceptionally long-lived and low-maintenance once established, resenting transplant once the taproot is set, and works well in a native prairie or meadow planting.

common_name: Appalachian Rosinweed (Cumberland Plateau Endemic Large-Leaf Silphium)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Appalachian Rosinweed is a Cumberland Plateau (Kentucky, Tennessee) endemic with large basal leaves, rarely seen in cultivation outside its native region.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; established plants tolerate drought well thanks to a deep taproot typical of the genus. Appalachian Rosinweed is a regional endemic restricted to the Cumberland Plateau of Kentucky and Tennessee, bearing large, coarse basal leaves and tall flowering stalks topped with bright yellow, sunflower-like composite blooms in summer, a rarely cultivated species that offers valuable genetic and regional diversity for native plant gardens within its home range. Like other Silphium species, its flowers draw specialist bees and other pollinators, and the seed heads that follow feed goldfinches and other birds. It is exceptionally long-lived and low-maintenance once established, resenting transplant once the taproot is set.

common_name: Giant Sunflower (Tall Wetland-Margin Native Perennial Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist to wet soil in full sun; Giant Sunflower is a tall (to 10 feet) native perennial sunflower of wet meadows and pond margins, blooming later than most native sunflower species.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, average soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or damp low spot. Giant Sunflower is an imposing native perennial sunflower reaching up to 10 feet tall, bearing numerous smaller flower heads than the familiar annual sunflower but in much greater number, blooming later in the season, from late summer into fall, than most other native perennial sunflowers, extending the pollinator nectar season. Its height and colony-forming spread by rhizomes make it best suited to a large naturalized wetland-edge planting or rain garden rather than a small formal border. The abundant seed heads that follow are a valuable fall and winter food source for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and maintain vigor.

common_name: Stiff Sunflower (Classic Tallgrass Prairie Rhizomatous Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Stiff Sunflower is a classic tallgrass-prairie species bearing fewer, larger flower heads than most native sunflowers, spreading by rhizomes and tolerant of drought.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; established plants tolerate considerable drought once their rhizomatous root system is settled. Stiff Sunflower is a defining species of the tallgrass prairie, bearing fewer but noticeably larger flower heads than most other native perennial sunflowers, on sturdy, upright, rough-textured stems that hold up well without staking. It spreads gradually by rhizomes to form an increasing colony, blooming from late summer into fall and providing valuable nectar and pollen for native bees and butterflies during a season when many spring bloomers have finished, followed by seed heads that feed goldfinches and other birds through fall and winter. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and low-maintenance, well suited to a native prairie planting or meadow garden. Divide congested colonies every few years in spring to control spread.

common_name: Resindot Sunflower (Clay-Tolerant Resin-Dotted Southeastern Perennial Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in average to clay soil in full sun to light partial shade; Resindot Sunflower is a southeastern US perennial with resin-dotted leaves, notably tolerant of heavier clay soils and some shade.

directions: Plant in average to clay-influenced soil in full sun to light partial shade; unusually tolerant of heavier, poorly drained soils and some shade compared to most native perennial sunflowers, which typically demand full sun and good drainage. Resindot Sunflower takes its name from the tiny resinous dots visible on the underside of its leaves, a distinguishing feature among Southeastern native sunflowers, bearing bright yellow, daisy-like blooms from late summer into fall that draw bees and butterflies. Its adaptability to clay soil makes it a practical native choice for gardens where drainage is less than ideal and other prairie natives struggle. Seed heads that follow provide food for goldfinches and other birds through fall and winter. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Sawtooth Sunflower (Very Tall Sharply Serrated Mesic Prairie Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist to average soil in full sun; Sawtooth Sunflower is a very tall (to 10-12 feet) native sunflower with sharply serrated leaves, a key late-season pollen and nectar source in mesic prairies.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; best sited at the back of a large native planting given its considerable height. Sawtooth Sunflower is one of the tallest native perennial sunflowers, reaching 10 to 12 feet in favorable conditions, with distinctively sharp, coarsely toothed leaves along smooth, waxy, blue-green stems, producing an abundance of bright yellow flower heads in late summer and fall that serve as a key late-season pollen and nectar resource in tallgrass prairie ecosystems. It spreads by rhizomes to form a substantial colony over time, best suited to a large meadow, prairie restoration, or naturalized area rather than a small formal bed. The abundant seed heads that follow feed goldfinches and other birds through fall and winter. Divide congested colonies every few years in spring to control spread.

common_name: Whiteleaf Sunflower (Southern Appalachian Endemic Woodland-Gap Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Whiteleaf Sunflower is a rare Southern Appalachian endemic with waxy, white-undersided leaves, adapted to woodland gaps rather than open prairie.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, in a woodland-edge or clearing setting rather than open prairie. Whiteleaf Sunflower is a rare endemic of the Southern Appalachian Mountains, considered vulnerable across its limited range, distinguished by leaves with a striking waxy, white-glaucous underside that contrasts sharply with the deep green upper surface, an ecologically distinct woodland-gap species among perennial sunflowers, most of which are open-prairie or meadow specialists. It bears typical bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads in late summer, drawing bees and butterflies, followed by seed heads valuable to goldfinches and other birds. Its shade tolerance makes it a useful native option for a woodland clearing or partly shaded native garden where open-prairie sunflower species would struggle. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Sandpaper Vervain (Rough Wetland and Tidal-Marsh Native Verbena)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet soil in full sun; Sandpaper Vervain is a wetland and tidal-marsh native with distinctly rough-textured leaves that extend down onto the stem, adapted to consistently damp conditions.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or low spot that stays reliably damp, since Sandpaper Vervain is native to wetland edges and even tidal freshwater marshes. Its leaves are notably rough and sandpaper-textured to the touch, tapering down and extending onto the stem in a way that distinguishes it from the drier-adapted native verbena species more commonly planted, bearing slender spikes of small pale lavender to white flowers from summer into fall that draw bees and butterflies. As a genuine wetland specialist, it fills a habitat niche that upland verbena species cannot, making it valuable for a rain garden, pond edge, or naturalized wet meadow planting. It self-sows readily in suitable damp conditions; thin seedlings as needed to control spread.

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Texas Grama is a small, tough native bunchgrass of Texas and Oklahoma with distinctive one-sided spike clusters, a larval host for several skipper and satyr butterflies.

directions: Direct sow in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Texas Grama tolerates poor, shallow, alkaline soils that defeat most turf grasses and ornamental perennials. This small, tough native bunchgrass of Texas and Oklahoma forms a low, fine-textured clump bearing distinctive comb-like, one-sided seed spikes on wiry stems in summer, adding subtle textural interest to a native prairie or xeriscape planting. It serves as a larval host plant for several native skipper and satyr butterfly species, adding wildlife value beyond its drought-tolerant, low-water landscaping role. It requires essentially no supplemental water or fertilizer once established and is well suited to rock gardens, dry meadow plantings, and low-water native landscaping. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Sand Dropseed (Extremely Drought-Tolerant Sandy-Soil Native Bunchgrass)

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; Sand Dropseed is a widespread, extremely drought-tolerant native bunchgrass of sandy soils, complementing the more ornamental prairie dropseed with even greater toughness in poor, dry sites.

directions: Direct sow in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; Sand Dropseed is among the most drought-tolerant native grasses available, thriving in loose, sandy, nutrient-poor soils where few other grasses persist. It forms an open, wiry-leaved clump topped by an airy, diffuse seed panicle in late summer that often breaks free and tumbles in the wind, dispersing seed widely, a distinct habit from the tighter, more formal seed heads of prairie dropseed already common in cultivation. Its extensive root system stabilizes loose, sandy, or eroding soil effectively, and the abundant small seeds are an important food source for songbirds and small mammals. It requires essentially no supplemental water or fertilizer once established, making it ideal for xeriscape plantings, dune stabilization, and low-water native landscaping. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring in moist to wet soil in full sun; Longspike Tridens is a tall (3-4 foot) wet-prairie native bunchgrass with dense, spike-like brownish-purple flower clusters, a seed source for birds and mammals and larval host for butterflies.

directions: Direct sow in consistently moist to wet, average soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or wet meadow site. Longspike Tridens forms an upright, clumping native bunchgrass reaching 3 to 4 feet, topped in late summer by dense, narrow, spike-like flower and seed clusters in a rich brownish-purple that stand out among the more typically airy or open panicles of other native grasses. As a genuine wet-prairie specialist, it fills a wet-soil niche that most ornamental grasses cannot tolerate, and its abundant seed provides food for birds and small mammals through fall and winter while also serving as a larval host plant for several native butterfly and skipper species. It requires little care beyond adequate moisture once established. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years if increase is wanted.
